content: 1. Syphilis is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by Treponema pallidum, which leads to significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. 2. The prevalence of syphilis is estimated to be 5 per 1000 males, with the highest rates observed among men aged 15–49 years, particularly in the WHO African Region. 3. Mother-to-child transmission of syphilis, also known as congenital syphilis, occurs when an infected pregnant woman transmits the infection to her fetus, often resulting in devastating outcomes if not detected and treated early in pregnancy. 4. In 2012, syphilis was estimated to cause approximately 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes globally, including 143,000 early fetal deaths or stillbirths, 62,000 neonatal deaths, 44,000 preterm or low-birth-weight infants, and 102,000 infected infants. 5. Pregnant women co-infected with syphilis and HIV are at an increased risk of transmitting HIV to their child. 6. Untreated primary and secondary syphilis infections during pregnancy frequently result in severe adverse outcomes, including fetal death in a substantial proportion of cases. 7. Latent syphilis infections during pregnancy are associated with serious adverse outcomes in more than half of cases. 8. The burden of syphilis is highest in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in the WHO African Region. 9. Congenital syphilis is preventable, and elimination of mother-to-child transmission of syphilis can be achieved through effective early screening and treatment strategies for pregnant women. 10. Early treatment of syphilis in pregnancy, ideally before the second trimester, significantly reduces the risk of adverse fetal outcomes, as the fetus can be easily cured with appropriate maternal treatment. 11. There is evidence that global efforts to screen and treat pregnant women for syphilis are beginning to reduce the rates of mother-to-child transmission of syphilis. 12. Diagnosis of syphilis relies on a combination of patient history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and sometimes radiological evaluation. 13. Many individuals with syphilis are asymptomatic or have only mild symptoms, making laboratory-based screening essential, particularly for pregnant women, to prevent further transmission and adverse outcomes. 14. Laboratory tests for syphilis include direct detection methods (e.g., dark-field microscopy, direct fluorescent antibody tests, nucleic acid amplification tests), serological tests (treponemal and non-treponemal), and cerebrospinal fluid analysis in specific cases. 15. Serological testing for syphilis involves two types of tests: non-treponemal tests (e.g., VDRL, RPR) and treponemal tests (e.g., TPHA, TPPA, FTA-ABS). A presumptive diagnosis requires a positive result from at least one test type, while a confirmed diagnosis requires positive results from both. 16. Non-treponemal tests are useful for monitoring treatment response, as titers typically decrease following effective treatment and increase in untreated active infections. 17. Treponemal tests are highly specific and detect antibodies against Treponema pallidum-specific antigens but cannot distinguish between active and previously treated infections. 18. Rapid syphilis tests (RSTs) have been developed to detect treponemal antibodies within 10–15 minutes and can be performed in various settings without the need for laboratory equipment or refrigeration. 19. Combined RSTs that detect both treponemal and non-treponemal antibodies are available but require further evaluation before widespread recommendation. 20. The WHO guidelines for syphilis screening and treatment emphasize early screening of pregnant women, ideally during the first antenatal care visit, to prevent mother-to-child transmission and adverse pregnancy outcomes. 21. Countries are encouraged to implement appropriate syphilis screening strategies to increase coverage and ensure that all pregnant women with syphilis receive adequate treatment. 22. The WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for syphilis screening and treatment in different healthcare settings, including the optimal sequence of tests and treatment approaches. 23. The guidelines aim to support countries in updating their national policies for syphilis screening and treatment, taking into account local laboratory infrastructure, healthcare capacity, and resources. 24. The development of these guidelines involved a multidisciplinary group of 33 international STI experts, including clinicians, researchers, and program managers, who reviewed evidence and finalized recommendations through meetings and teleconferences. 25. The guidelines are intended for healthcare providers at all levels of the healthcare system, as well as policymakers and program managers responsible for implementing STI management interventions globally.
